prize_parts.citation: for empirical evidence on how import competition and technological change shape labour demand and the adjustment of local labour markets

statement.case_for: My laureate set is unchanged from round 1: Autor, Dorn and Hanson for B036. I have changed the citation. It now rests on exposure and adjustment evidence, with no reference to wage inequality as a settled outcome and no claim about effect size. This responds to the chair's wording question and to the repeated point that the size and persistence of the effects are unresolved. My main criterion is whether a claim has been exposed to re-analysis and has survived. The China-shock designs are transparent enough that many groups re-examined them, with different exposure measures, different inference, different samples and different countries. The core finding survived in qualified form: import exposure produced concentrated, slow local adjustment, while the magnitudes were revised. That record is stronger than for several candidates whose central estimates rest on a single model or on assumptions that are hard to test. I treat this as a judgment about the evidence base, not as a count of support. Seven preferred configurations now name the same trio, but several of those positions were revised during round 1, so I do not read the count as independent confirmation. The attribution is the cleanest available: the empirical programme is jointly authored by the three, and Autor's own work links the task framework to the trade evidence. That is why I do not add task-framework authors. A scope statement in the citation would keep it from being read as a ruling on the origins of the task framework.
statement.case_against: The reservations I take most seriously are three. First, the long-run size and persistence of the effects, and the shift-share identification behind the exposure measures, are still debated. If a careful review showed that the core local employment effect is fragile to alternative exposure measures or inference, my view on maturity would change. Second, the ballot entry bundles two literatures, and this configuration leaves Katz and the task lineage uncredited. Part of that lineage involves Acemoglu, who is outside the credited set and was recognised in 2024, and Levy and Murnane. That cost is real and a narrow citation does not remove it. Third, the 2021 and 2023 labour prizes and the 2024 technology-and-institutions prize overlap thematically, which may leave the Committee feeling the slot is less open. I also have a possible bias. My own field values replication and re-examination, so I may give extra weight to a literature that invited scrutiny. I have tried to apply the same test to B003, B002 and B034, and the structural or model-dependent candidates do worse on it, not better.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B036 seventh and questions whether the maturity bar is met, because identification, persistence and the magnitude of the China shock are still debated and the technology side overlaps with Acemoglu's recognised work. He says he would not oppose it, and that B020 is not clearly weaker once the magnitude dispute is counted.
responses.response: I take the maturity question seriously, and I would put it differently from how I did in round 1. The test is whether a discovery has been exposed to hostile re-analysis and what survived. For B036 the answer is a qualified yes: the sign and local concentration of the effects have held, and the magnitudes have been revised. I agree that this is not the same as the long-run aggregate size being settled, so the citation should not claim it. I would also apply your point about structural estimates being sensitive to instruments and functional form with the same strictness to B020. Your own file concedes it, and I do not think it separates B020 from B036 in B020's favour. Where we differ is mainly on how much weight the methods-versus-discovery distinction deserves. I do not count that distinction against B020 as strongly as some colleagues do. My concern is that its credit is split between the demand and dynamics strands. A specific finding would move me: evidence that the core local employment effect fails under reasonable alternative exposure measures. The shift-share critiques as I know them refine inference and instrument validity, and I have not independently verified that.

responses.point: Enflo prefers B034 with Helpman and Melitz. She says my own and Hjalmarsson's reading that the China-shock findings have held up is too generous, because exposure measures, persistence and automation are still debated. She adds that B034 has no comparable dispute over magnitudes and no recent adjacent prize.
responses.response: I accept the correction in part. 'Held up' is too strong, and I now say 'survived in qualified form'. I do not think the absence of a magnitude dispute in B034 is evidence of robustness. The welfare gains there depend on model structure and parametrisation, as you and Strömberg both note. A result can look undisputed because it has been tested less directly. The selection mechanism has been confronted with firm-level data, but not through the kind of design-based re-examination that the China-shock estimates received. The 2008 overlap and the Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum priority question are also separate problems that B036 does not have in the same form. I do not dismiss B034. The attribution to Melitz is clean, and I would not oppose it on scientific grounds. On the criterion I weight most, the transparency of the evidence and how well it was stress-tested, I still rank B036 higher.

responses.point: Krusell prefers B018 with Calvo, Taylor and Woodford. He keeps B036 as his first alternative, and says that persistence and identification are contested and that the work overlaps with the 2024 prize. He also concedes that credit for B018 is spread across at least eight people.
responses.response: I agree that the B036 effects are contested and that the 2024 overlap is thematic and worth weighing. The difference between us seems to be how the two contested records compare. B018 is much older and its importance is not in doubt. The post-2008 and 2021-23 debates test the framework rather than refute it, as you say. I do not think B018's contested record is any more settled than B036's. The decisive point for me is that B018's three-name cut is the weakest part of its case, and your own file records that the cut cannot be fixed by choosing Taylor or Galí as third. For B036, the credited trio matches the authorship of the core papers. That is a structural advantage, not a statement that B018 is less important. If the Committee found a defensible founding credit for B018, I would reassess it. I ranked it fifth in my opening and have not moved it.

responses.point: Teorell now prefers B036 with Autor, Dorn and Hanson. He wants the Committee to review the shift-share exposure critiques before finalising and says the citation should credit local labour-market adjustment evidence, not a particular elasticity. He also notes that the task and trade strands are distinct and the bundling is the weak point.
responses.response: I agree with the citation point and have worded mine that way. On your proposed review, I would suggest the Committee check three things: whether the local employment effect holds under alternative exposure measures and inference methods, whether persistence findings hold across countries and designs, and whether the automation-versus-trade attribution changes the interpretation. I would treat the first as the most important for maturity. On bundling, I still think Autor spans both strands, which is a reason to name him and not to add task-framework authors. I agree with you that the citation should say plainly what it does not cover, to avoid a reading that the Committee has settled who originated the task framework. I can answer the question the chair raised about what the technology strand adds beyond 2023 and 2024 only partly: it adds evidence on how exposure and automation shape labour demand, not the theory of tasks, and I think the Committee should state that distinction openly.

uncertainties: Whether the core local employment and persistence findings survive a systematic review of the shift-share exposure critiques, which I have not independently verified.
Whether leaving out Katz and the task lineage, including originators outside the credited set, is an acceptable attribution cost under a narrowly worded citation.
How much room the 2021, 2023 and 2024 prizes leave for another award on labour demand, technology and trade.

Whether B003 or B002 would be preferred if the Committee judged B036 too contested or too heterogeneous. B003 has its own attribution questions (Saez and Chetty appear on other ballots, and the credited names go beyond a pair), and I have not tested it as hard as B036.

My assessment relies on the supplied round-1 files and my own knowledge of the literature, without independent verification of attributions. My metascience orientation may lead me to over-weight transparent, re-examined evidence.
statement.conflict_note: No change. None apparent from the supplied profile. Autor, Dorn and Hanson, and the alternatives' credited names (Saez, Slemrod, Chetty, Stantcheva; Manski, Tamer, Molinari), do not appear among my listed co-authors or institutional contacts. My JPE editorial roles (Associate Editor 2018-2026, JPE Microeconomics Editor 2022-April 2026) are generic and not a link to any credited person that I can identify. I disclose field proximity to replication and metascience, which may incline me toward work that invited re-examination. Conflicts are disclosed here, not adjudicated.
